headline: High risk of shared-repo prompt injection and capability conflict; no direct data-leak path is evidenced.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Aider writes to and reads from a shared git repo, so attacker-controlled repo content can be fed back into its prompts. awesome-prompts is a content-writing prompt repository, so if its contents are copied into the same workspace or used as instructions, Aider can be steered. The pair lacks direct shared-channel evidence, so I do not escalate to high.
conditions: IF awesome-prompts content is placed in the same git workspace as Aider inputs, prompt injection is possible.
IF Aider treats repository text as instructions rather than data, malicious prompt content can steer behavior.
mitigations: Keep prompt repositories in a separate directory from Aider's working repo.
Review copied prompt text before pasting it into Aider.
Use a read-only clone for prompt browsing.
Add a manual instruction/data separator in operator workflow.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for repo-derived text.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Aider touches source code and git history and can send context to configured model providers, but awesome-prompts is non-runnable and has no filesystem or network surface. There is no documented shared workspace or credential bridge between the pair, so leakage from Aider into awesome-prompts is limited to operator-mediated copying.
conditions: IF the operator copies source code or git history from Aider into awesome-prompts content, that data can be exposed.
IF Aider is configured with a third-party model provider, its context may leave the local machine.
mitigations: Do not paste secrets or code into prompt-list content.
Use redacted snippets when transferring text between tools.
Keep Aider API keys scoped to the minimum needed.
Audit copied content before publishing it.
requires-engineering: enforce workspace isolation between code and prompt repositories.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Aider has unrestricted filesystem write and git-state modification in a shared repo, while awesome-prompts is a content-writing repository that can also be edited by the operator. That creates overlapping mutable state if both are used on the same repo or branch. The conflict is plausible in default coding workflows, though not proven to be simultaneous by the profiles.
conditions: IF both agents are used against the same git repository, concurrent edits can collide.
IF the operator commits prompt content and code changes in one branch, git conflicts can occur.
mitigations: Use separate branches for code and prompt content.
Pull and rebase before each edit session.
Avoid concurrent edits to the same files.
Assign one agent per repository checkout.
requires-engineering: add locking around shared git state.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Aider can generate or edit code, but awesome-prompts is a static prompt collection and does not act on Aider's output. There is no evidence that B consumes A's outputs automatically or performs downstream actions, so the cascade is mostly manual and limited to operator misuse.
conditions: IF the operator copies Aider-generated text into awesome-prompts without review, errors can propagate.
IF the prompt repository is later used as authoritative guidance, bad instructions can be reused.
mitigations: Manually review Aider output before reusing it.
Keep generated code and prompt text in separate files.
Mark unverified prompt content clearly.
Use a second reviewer for copied instructions.
requires-engineering: add validation for prompt provenance.

E_compliance.rationale: Aider handles source code, git history, and model-provider API keys, which can create compliance obligations, but awesome-prompts is a public content repository with no declared sensitive-data handling. The pair does not show a residency or regulated-data mismatch, so the main issue is limited policy drift rather than a breach.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into Aider's repo, provider and retention policies become relevant.
IF prompt content is published from a controlled environment, internal-policy violations can occur.
mitigations: Do not store regulated data in the repo.
Confirm provider retention settings before use.
Publish only non-sensitive prompt content.
Document data-class boundaries for operators.
requires-engineering: add compliance gating for sensitive repositories.
